lexemes.note: The first month of the civil (Gregorian) year. “In January” = בְּיָנוּאָר (no article); a date: day + בְּ + month (אֶחָד בְּיָנוּאָר).

override.pos: Wiktionary files the Gregorian month names as proper nouns (“name”); the course treats them as nouns, like the month names of its other languages.

profile.feeling: Rain in Tel Aviv, snow on the Hermon, the civil New Year.

examples.tr: The civil year begins on the first of January.
In January there is snow on Mount Hermon.
My birthday is in January.

etymology.text: From German Januar, from Latin Iānuārius “(month) of Janus” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Like the other month names, Hebrew took יָנוּאָר from German (Wiktionary) — so German Januar, Russian январь and Greek Ιανουάριος are its brothers.
pitfalls: No article and no change after בְּ: בְּיָנוּאָר “in January” (a month is like a name).
The Jewish New Year (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה) is in the autumn; 1 January is the civil New Year, often called סִילְבֶסְטֶר for its eve.
subtleties: January falls in the Hebrew months טֵבֵת and שְׁבָט; Hebrew dates and Gregorian dates are both used in Israel.

lexemes.note: The second month of the civil (Gregorian) year. “In February” = בְּפֶבְּרוּאָר (no article); a date: day + בְּ + month (אֶחָד בְּפֶבְּרוּאָר).

override.pos: Wiktionary files the Gregorian month names as proper nouns (“name”); the course treats them as nouns, like the month names of its other languages.

profile.feeling: The short month; almond trees in bloom.

examples.tr: February has twenty-eight days.

examples.text: טוּ בִּשְׁבָט חָל בְּיָנוּאָר אוֹ בְּפֶבְּרוּאָר.
examples.tr: Tu BiShvat falls in January or February.
The almond trees bloom in February.

etymology.text: From German Februar, from Latin Februarius (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Turkish Şubat and Levantine Arabic شُبَاط “February” carry the old Semitic month name that Hebrew calls שְׁבָט.
pitfalls: The first letter is פ without a dot: f (februar) — a sign of a loanword.
No article and no change after בְּ: בְּפֶבְּרוּאָר “in February” (a month is like a name).
subtleties: February overlaps the Hebrew month שְׁבָט; the tree festival טוּ בִּשְׁבָט (15 Shevat) falls in January or February.

lexemes.note: The third month of the civil (Gregorian) year. “In March” = בְּמֶרְץ (no article); a date: day + בְּ + month (אֶחָד בְּמֶרְץ).

override.meaning: The only noun Wiktionary files under the letters מרץ is מֶרֶץ “energy, vigour”, another word; the month מֶרְץ “March” is filed there as a proper noun (name), with exactly this vowelling.
override.N;SG;INDF: Wiktionary’s vowelling מֶרֶץ belongs to the other word under these letters (“energy”); its entry for the month “March” is vowelled מֶרְץ, as here.

profile.feeling: Spring arrives; Purim costumes.

examples.tr: Spring begins in March.
Purim usually falls in March.
The course starts on the twentieth of March.

synonyms.nuance: another spelling and pronunciation (מרס / מארס), less common (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: Borrowed from German März, from Latin Martius (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Levantine Arabic آذَار “March” is the old month name that Hebrew calls אֲדָר.
pitfalls: Unvowelled מרץ is also מֶרֶץ “energy, vigour” (Wiktionary) — read it by the context.
No article and no change after בְּ: בְּמֶרְץ “in March” (a month is like a name).
subtleties: March overlaps the Hebrew month אֲדָר (Purim, 14 Adar) or נִיסָן. In a Hebrew leap year there are two Adars: אֲדָר א׳ and אֲדָר ב׳.

lexemes.note: The fourth month of the civil (Gregorian) year. “In April” = בְּאַפְּרִיל (no article); a date: day + בְּ + month (אֶחָד בְּאַפְּרִיל).

override.pos: Wiktionary files the Gregorian month names as proper nouns (“name”); the course treats them as nouns, like the month names of its other languages.

profile.feeling: Passover, spring flowers, April fools.

examples.tr: Passover usually falls in April.
In April we travel up north.
April fool! (the first of April)

etymology.text: From German April, from Latin Aprilis (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Turkish Nisan “April” and Levantine Arabic نَيْسَان are the same name as the Hebrew month נִיסָן.
pitfalls: No article and no change after בְּ: בְּאַפְּרִיל “in April” (a month is like a name).
אֶחָד בְּאַפְּרִיל is April Fools’ Day — and the shout “April fool!” (Wiktionary).
subtleties: April overlaps the Hebrew month נִיסָן, the month of Passover (פֶּסַח, 15 Nisan).

lexemes.note: The fifth month of the civil (Gregorian) year. “In May” = בְּמַאי (no article); a date: day + בְּ + month (אֶחָד בְּמַאי).

override.pos: Wiktionary files the Gregorian month names as proper nouns (“name”); the course treats them as nouns, like the month names of its other languages.

profile.feeling: Warm days, Independence Day barbecues.

examples.tr: In May it is already hot.

examples.text: יוֹם הָעַצְמָאוּת חָל בְּאַפְּרִיל אוֹ בְּמַאי.
examples.tr: Independence Day falls in April or May.
The first of May is Labour Day.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; Wiktionary gives no abbreviation for this short name.

etymology.text: From German Mai, from Latin Māius “Maia’s month” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Levantine Arabic أَيَّار “May” is the old month name that Hebrew calls אִיָּר.
pitfalls: No article and no change after בְּ: בְּמַאי “in May” (a month is like a name).
Unvowelled מאי is also a girl’s name, and in the Talmud the Aramaic מַאי “what?” (Wiktionary).
subtleties: May overlaps the Hebrew month אִיָּר, when Israel’s Independence Day (5 Iyar) is celebrated.

lexemes.note: The sixth month of the civil (Gregorian) year. “In June” = בְּיוּנִי (no article); a date: day + בְּ + month (אֶחָד בְּיוּנִי).

override.meaning: The nouns Wiktionary files under the letters יוני are other words (יוֹנֵי־ “doves of”, יְוָנִי “Greek”); the month יוּנִי “June” is filed there as a proper noun (name).

profile.feeling: The end of the school year, long hot days.

examples.tr: In June the school year ends.
Shavuot falls in May or June.
The holiday starts at the end of June.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; Wiktionary gives no abbreviation for this short name.

etymology.text: From German Juni, from Latin Iunius (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Unvowelled, “June” and “Greek” (יוני / יווני) are almost the same word — a pun for a Greek speaker.
pitfalls: No article and no change after בְּ: בְּיוּנִי “in June” (a month is like a name).
Unvowelled יוני is also the boy’s name Yoni, and יְוָנִי “Greek” in short spelling (Wiktionary) — vowels or context decide.
subtleties: June overlaps the Hebrew month סִיוָן, the month of Shavuot (6 Sivan).

lexemes.note: The seventh month of the civil (Gregorian) year. “In July” = בְּיוּלִי (no article); a date: day + בְּ + month (אֶחָד בְּיוּלִי).

override.pos: Wiktionary files the Gregorian month names as proper nouns (“name”); the course treats them as nouns, like the month names of its other languages.

profile.feeling: The heat of the summer holiday.

examples.tr: In July we go to the sea.

examples.text: יוּלִי וְאוֹגוּסְט הֵם הַחֳדָשִׁים הַחַמִּים בְּיוֹתֵר.
examples.tr: July and August are the hottest months.
The summer camp starts on the first of July.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; Wiktionary gives no abbreviation for this short name.

etymology.text: From German Juli, from Latin Iulius (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Turkish Temmuz “July” and Levantine Arabic تَمُّوز are the same name as the Hebrew month תַּמּוּז.
pitfalls: No article and no change after בְּ: בְּיוּלִי “in July” (a month is like a name).
Unvowelled יולי is also a given name (Wiktionary).
subtleties: July overlaps the Hebrew month תַּמּוּז.

lexemes.note: The eighth month of the civil (Gregorian) year. “In August” = בְּאוֹגוּסְט (no article); a date: day + בְּ + month (אֶחָד בְּאוֹגוּסְט).

override.pos: Wiktionary files the Gregorian month names as proper nouns (“name”); the course treats them as nouns, like the month names of its other languages.

profile.feeling: Beaches, family trips, the hottest weeks.

examples.tr: In August it is very hot.
Our holiday is in August.

examples.text: תִּשְׁעָה בְּאָב חָל בְּיוּלִי אוֹ בְּאוֹגוּסְט.
examples.tr: Tisha B’Av falls in July or August.

etymology.text: From German August, from Latin Augustus; the pronunciation was likely influenced by English August (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Levantine Arabic آب “August” is the same name as the Hebrew month אָב.
pitfalls: No article and no change after בְּ: בְּאוֹגוּסְט “in August” (a month is like a name).
Stress on the first syllable: ógust.
subtleties: August overlaps the Hebrew month אָב (Tisha B’Av, 9 Av, the fast for the Temple).

lexemes.note: The ninth month of the civil (Gregorian) year. “In September” = בְּסֶפְּטֶמְבֶּר (no article); a date: day + בְּ + month (אֶחָד בְּסֶפְּטֶמְבֶּר).

override.pos: Wiktionary files the Gregorian month names as proper nouns (“name”); the course treats them as nouns, like the month names of its other languages.

profile.feeling: Back to school and the Jewish New Year.

examples.text: בְּאֶחָד בְּסֶפְּטֶמְבֶּר הַיְּלָדִים חוֹזְרִים לְבֵית הַסֵּפֶר.
examples.tr: On the first of September the children go back to school.

examples.text: רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה חָל בְּסֶפְּטֶמְבֶּר אוֹ בְּאוֹקְטוֹבֶּר.
examples.tr: Rosh Hashana falls in September or October.
He is coming back from abroad in September.

collocations.tr: the first of September (the first school day)

etymology.text: Borrowed from German September, from Latin September (Wiktionary) — from septem “seven”: the seventh month of the old Roman year.

funFacts: Turkish Eylül “September” and Levantine Arabic أَيْلُول are the same name as the Hebrew month אֱלוּל.
pitfalls: No article and no change after בְּ: בְּסֶפְּטֶמְבֶּר “in September” (a month is like a name).
The school year in Israel starts on 1 September.
subtleties: September overlaps the Hebrew months אֱלוּל and תִּשְׁרֵי — the time of the High Holidays.

lexemes.note: The tenth month of the civil (Gregorian) year. “In October” = בְּאוֹקְטוֹבֶּר (no article); a date: day + בְּ + month (אֶחָד בְּאוֹקְטוֹבֶּר).

override.pos: Wiktionary files the Gregorian month names as proper nouns (“name”); the course treats them as nouns, like the month names of its other languages.

profile.feeling: Sukkot booths, the first rain.

examples.tr: In October the students go back to university.
Sukkot falls in September or October.
The first rain falls in October.

etymology.text: Borrowed from German Oktober, from Latin October (Wiktionary) — from octo “eight”: the eighth month of the old Roman year.

funFacts: Levantine Arabic تِشْرِين الْأَوَّل “October” carries the old name that Hebrew calls תִּשְׁרֵי.
pitfalls: No article and no change after בְּ: בְּאוֹקְטוֹבֶּר “in October” (a month is like a name).
Israeli universities start the year in October, after the autumn holidays.
subtleties: October overlaps the Hebrew months תִּשְׁרֵי and חֶשְׁוָן.

lexemes.note: The eleventh month of the civil (Gregorian) year. “In November” = בְּנוֹבֶמְבֶּר (no article); a date: day + בְּ + month (אֶחָד בְּנוֹבֶמְבֶּר).

override.pos: Wiktionary files the Gregorian month names as proper nouns (“name”); the course treats them as nouns, like the month names of its other languages.

profile.feeling: Rain and the first cool evenings.

examples.tr: Her birthday is in November.
In November it rains a lot.
They live on 29 November Street.

collocations.tr: 29 November (the UN vote of 1947; a street name)

etymology.text: From German November, from Latin November (Wiktionary) — from novem “nine”: the ninth month of the old Roman year.

funFacts: Many Israeli towns have a street called כ״ט בְּנוֹבֶמְבֶּר, after the UN vote of 29 November 1947 on the partition of Palestine.
pitfalls: No article and no change after בְּ: בְּנוֹבֶמְבֶּר “in November” (a month is like a name).
In כ״ט בְּנוֹבֶמְבֶּר the day is written with Hebrew letters (כ״ט = 29) — read it “kaf-tet be-november”.
subtleties: November overlaps the Hebrew months חֶשְׁוָן and כִּסְלֵו.

lexemes.note: The twelfth month of the civil (Gregorian) year. “In December” = בְּדֵצֶמְבֶּר (no article); a date: day + בְּ + month (אֶחָד בְּדֵצֶמְבֶּר).

override.pos: Wiktionary files the Gregorian month names as proper nouns (“name”); the course treats them as nouns, like the month names of its other languages.

profile.feeling: Hanukkah candles, short days.

examples.text: חֲנֻכָּה חָל בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל בְּחֹדֶשׁ דֵּצֶמְבֶּר.
examples.tr: Hanukkah usually falls in December.
December is the last month of the year.
The office is closed until the end of December.

collocations.tr: in December (the ד loses its dot: bedetsember)

etymology.text: From German Dezember, from Latin december “tenth month”, from decem “ten”: December was the tenth month of the Roman calendar (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Latin decem “ten” is the same word as Greek δέκα and Russian десять — December was the tenth month (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: After בְּ the dot of the ד disappears: בְּדֵצֶמְבֶּר (bedetsember).
No article: בְּדֵצֶמְבֶּר “in December”.
subtleties: December overlaps the Hebrew months כִּסְלֵו and טֵבֵת; Hanukkah begins on 25 Kislev.

lexemes.note: “In spring” = בָּאָבִיב (with the article).

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ / לָ (בְּ / לְ + the article), which drop the ה of the article: הָאָבִיב → (בַּ / לַ)אָבִיב; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הָאָבִיב.

profile.feeling: Green fields and wild flowers — short and lovely.

senses.def: fresh ears of barley; the early ripening of grain

examples.tr: In spring the fields are green.
Passover is the festival of spring.
Spring in Israel is short.

etymology.text: From a root meaning “to be thick, swell, ripen”; possibly cognate with Arabic أَبّ (ʔabb, “pasture, herbage”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Tel Aviv, תֵּל אָבִיב, is “the hill of spring” — the Hebrew title of Herzl’s novel Altneuland, from a place name in Ezekiel 3:15.
pitfalls: “In spring” takes the article: בָּאָבִיב (not *בְּאָבִיב).
Masculine: אָבִיב חַם “a warm spring”.
subtleties: In the Bible אָבִיב is fresh barley, and חֹדֶשׁ הָאָבִיב the month of Nisan (Wiktionary).

lexemes.note: “In summer” = בַּקַּיִץ. Plural קֵיצִים.

profile.feeling: Long, hot and humid; the beach and the big holiday.

examples.tr: In summer it is very hot.
In summer we go to the sea.
The summer holiday starts in July.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *qayθ̣- “summer”; compare Aramaic qēṭā and Arabic قَيْظ (qayẓ, “oppressive heat, midsummer”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Arabic cousin قَيْظ means the fierce midsummer heat; the ordinary Arabic “summer” is another word, صَيْف.
pitfalls: “In summer” takes the article: בַּקַּיִץ.
A segolate noun: קַיִץ, but the plural is קֵיצִים.
subtleties: קֵיצִי “summery” (Wiktionary) — בְּגָדִים קֵיצִיִּים “summer clothes”.

lexemes.note: “In autumn” = בַּסְּתָו. Written without vowels סתיו (with a silent י).

profile.feeling: The first rain, the autumn holidays.

examples.tr: In autumn the rain begins.
The holidays of Tishrei are in the autumn.
For lo, the winter is past.

phrases.tr: for lo, the winter is past
phrases.meaning: the bad season is over; spring has come

etymology.text: Compare Arabic شِتَاء (šitāʔ, “winter”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: A false friend between the course’s two Semitic languages: Hebrew סְתָו is autumn, its Arabic cousin شِتَاء is winter — and Hebrew חֹרֶף “winter” matches Arabic خَرِيف “autumn” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Written without vowels סתיו (with י), as in the name Stav (Wiktionary).
“In autumn” takes the article: בַּסְּתָו.
subtleties: In the Bible סְתָו is the rainy winter (Wiktionary): כִּי הִנֵּה הַסְּתָו עָבָר “for lo, the winter is past” (Song of Songs 2:11).

lexemes.note: “In winter” = בַּחֹרֶף. Full spelling חורף.

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ / לָ (בְּ / לְ + the article), which drop the ה of the article: הַחֹרֶף → (בַּ / לַ)חֹרֶף; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הַחֹרֶף.

profile.feeling: Rain, a heater, soup — and snow in Jerusalem now and then.

examples.tr: In winter it rains.
In winter it is cold in Jerusalem.
I (m.) need a winter coat.

etymology.text: Cognate with Arabic خَرِيف (ḵarīf, “autumn, fall”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic خَرِيف is the same word but means autumn: the seasons “moved” between the two languages (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: “In winter” takes the article: בַּחֹרֶף.
Plural חֳרָפִים; full spelling חורף.
subtleties: חָרְפִּי “wintry” (Wiktionary).

lexemes.note: “This week” = הַשָּׁבוּעַ. Two weeks = שְׁבוּעַיִם (dual). Plural שָׁבוּעוֹת (masculine, with -וֹת).

profile.feeling: Seven days, from Sunday to Shabbat.

examples.tr: There are seven days in a week.
This week I (m.) am working from home.
Have a good week! (said on Saturday night)

phrases.meaning: have a good week (greeting on Saturday night)

etymology.text: Related to שֶׁבַע “seven” (Wiktionary): a period of seven days.

funFacts: The festival of Shavuot, שָׁבוּעוֹת, is literally “Weeks”: it comes seven weeks after Passover.
pitfalls: Masculine, but the plural is שָׁבוּעוֹת.
Two weeks is the dual שְׁבוּעַיִם, not *שְׁנֵי שָׁבוּעוֹת.
“This week” is הַשָּׁבוּעַ — the article alone.
subtleties: שָׁבוּעַ טוֹב “a good week” is the greeting when Shabbat ends on Saturday evening.

lexemes.note: “This month” = הַחֹדֶשׁ. Two months = חׇדְשַׁיִם (dual). Full spelling חודש.

profile.feeling: Rent, salary, the new moon.

senses.def: new moon, the first day of a Hebrew month

examples.tr: There are twelve months in a year.
This month we are on holiday.
the new moon of Elul

etymology.text: Originally “new moon”; related to חָדָשׁ “new”; compare Phoenician ḥdš “new moon, month” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: A month is a “new (moon)”: חֹדֶשׁ and חָדָשׁ “new” are one root (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Plural חֳדָשִׁים (khodashim); two months = חׇדְשַׁיִם.
Do not confuse with חָדָשׁ “new” — same letters, other vowels.
subtleties: The Hebrew calendar is lunar: every month begins with the new moon, רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ “head of the month”.

lexemes.note: Feminine, but the plural is שָׁנִים. “This year” = הַשָּׁנָה. Two years = שְׁנָתַיִם.

profile.feeling: Birthdays, anniversaries, “a good year!”.

examples.tr: Happy New Year! (“a good year”)
This year we are travelling to Greece.
He has lived here for twenty years.

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šanat-; cognate with Arabic سَنَة (sana) and Ugaritic šnt (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic سَنَة (sana) is the same word (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Feminine (שָׁנָה טוֹבָה) but the plural ends in -ִים: שָׁנִים.
Unvowelled שנה is also שֵׁנָה “sleep” and the verb שָׁנָה “repeated” (Wiktionary).
subtleties: After numbers from eleven on, time words often stay singular: עֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה “twenty years”.
רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה “the head of the year” is the Jewish New Year, in September or October.

lexemes.note: Hour, and the word for telling the time: הַשָּׁעָה שָׁלוֹשׁ “it is three o’clock”, בְּשָׁעָה שָׁלוֹשׁ “at three o’clock” — with the feminine numbers. Two hours = שְׁעָתַיִם.

profile.feeling: Clocks, timetables, “what time is it?”.

senses.def: o’clock, the time on the clock (הַשָּׁעָה + number)
a time, a moment (בְּשָׁעָה טוֹבָה “at a good time”)

examples.tr: The trip to Haifa takes an hour.
I (m.) have been waiting for two hours.
What time is it?
It is three o’clock.
The train leaves at five o’clock.

phrases.meaning: congratulations (on a birth, a new step); may it be at a lucky time

phrases.tr: the small hours of the night

synonyms.nuance: “time” in general: אֵין לִי זְמַן “I have no time” — not the time on the clock

etymology.text: From Aramaic šāʿəṯā; cognate with Arabic سَاعَة (sāʕa) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic سَاعَة and Turkish saat (from Arabic) mean both “hour” and “clock” — Hebrew uses שָׁעָה for the hour and שָׁעוֹן for the clock.
pitfalls: Telling the time uses the feminine numbers, because שָׁעָה is feminine: הַשָּׁעָה שָׁלוֹשׁ (not שְׁלוֹשָׁה), בְּשָׁעָה שְׁתַּיִם.
There is no separate word for “o’clock”: “at five o’clock” is בְּשָׁעָה חָמֵשׁ (or just בְּחָמֵשׁ).
Two hours = שְׁעָתַיִם (dual), not *שְׁתֵּי שָׁעוֹת.
subtleties: Half past = וָחֵצִי: הַשָּׁעָה שָׁלוֹשׁ וָחֵצִי; quarter past = וָרֶבַע; quarter to = רֶבַע לְ…: רֶבַע לְאַרְבַּע.
A watch or a clock is a שָׁעוֹן — from שָׁעָה (Wiktionary).

profile.feeling: “Just a minute!”

examples.tr: It’s ten minutes on foot.
There are sixty minutes in an hour.
Wait a minute! (to a man)

synonyms.nuance: “a moment”: רֶגַע! “just a moment!” — not a measured minute

etymology.text: Compare Arabic دَقِيقَة (daqīqa) (Wiktionary) — the root of דַּק “thin, fine”: a small part (of the hour).

funFacts: Arabic دَقِيقَة and Turkish dakika are the same word — the “fine, small” part of an hour (Wiktionary gives the Arabic).
pitfalls: Feminine: דַּקָּה אַחַת, חָמֵשׁ דַּקּוֹת (feminine numbers).
Unvowelled דקה is also דַּקָּה “thin (f.)” — the adjective דַּק (Wiktionary).
subtleties: עוֹד דַּקָּה is “in a minute”; רֶגַע is shorter and vaguer.

profile.feeling: Forms, deadlines, the top of a letter.

examples.tr: What’s the date today?
Write the date at the top of the page.
What is the milk’s expiry date?

etymology.text: Borrowed from Arabic تَأْرِيخ (taʔrīḵ, “date”); ultimately from Proto-Semitic *warḫ- “moon, month” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic تَارِيخ and Turkish tarih mean both “date” and “history”; Hebrew borrowed only “date”.
pitfalls: A date is a day of the calendar — not a meeting with someone (that is פְּגִישָׁה) and not the fruit (תָּמָר).
Masculine: תַּאֲרִיךְ חָשׁוּב.
subtleties: A date is said “day + בְּ + month”: עֶשְׂרִים בְּמַאי “the 20th of May” (masculine numbers, for יוֹם).

lexemes.note: The article goes on the second word: יוֹם הַהֻלֶּדֶת שֶׁלִּי “my birthday”. Plural יְמֵי הֻלֶּדֶת.

profile.feeling: Cake, candles, the whole family singing.

examples.tr: Happy birthday!
When is your (m.) birthday?
My birthday is in May.

phrases.meaning: a birthday wish: a long life, like Moses’ 120 years

etymology.text: יוֹם “day” + הֻלֶּדֶת “birth” (Wiktionary has both words); “day of birth”.

funFacts: Israelis also sing יוֹם הֻלֶּדֶת שָׂמֵחַ to the English tune of “Happy Birthday”.
pitfalls: The article goes on the second word: יוֹם הַהֻלֶּדֶת (not *הַיּוֹם הֻלֶּדֶת).
Plural יְמֵי הֻלֶּדֶת.
subtleties: The traditional wish is עַד מֵאָה וְעֶשְׂרִים “(may you live) to a hundred and twenty”, like Moses.

lexemes.note: A holiday, time off (from work or school). A religious or national holiday is חַג. Full spelling חופשה.

profile.feeling: Days off: a trip abroad, a week by the sea.

examples.tr: We are on holiday!
Have a nice holiday!
He is taking a week off.

synonyms.nuance: “holiday, time off”, especially from school: הַחֹפֶשׁ הַגָּדוֹל “the long summer holiday” (Wiktionary)
“a festival, a public holiday” (Passover, Independence Day) — not your own time off

etymology.text: From the root ח־פ־שׁ “free” (חֹפֶשׁ “freedom”, חָפְשִׁי “free”); Wiktionary gives no etymology of its own.

funFacts: A holiday is “freedom”: חֻפְשָׁה, חֹפֶשׁ and חָפְשִׁי “free” share one root.
pitfalls: Your own days off are חֻפְשָׁה; a festival is חַג: חַג שָׂמֵחַ!
Full spelling חופשה (qubuts → ו).
subtleties: In the summer children have the חֹפֶשׁ הַגָּדוֹל, “the big holiday”, July and August.

lexemes.note: “After” (in time): אַחֲרֵי הָעֲבוֹדָה. Before a clause אַחֲרֵי שֶׁ…; with pronouns אַחֲרַי “after me”, אַחֲרֶיךָ …

profile.feeling: What comes next: after work, after dinner.

examples.tr: After work I (m.) go to the park.

examples.text: אַחֲרֵי אֲרוּחַת הָעֶרֶב אֲנַחְנוּ שׁוֹתִים תֵּה.
examples.tr: After dinner we drink tea.
He is running after the bus.

synonyms.nuance: “after” in writing and the news (Wiktionary lists it as related)

etymology.text: Related to אַחַר and לְאַחַר (Wiktionary, which gives no etymology of its own); from the root א־ח־ר “behind, after”.

funFacts: The same root gives אַחֲרוֹן “last”, מְאֻחָר “late” and אַחֲרָיוּת “responsibility” — what comes “after” you.
pitfalls: “After” + a noun is אַחֲרֵי; “afterwards” alone is אַחַר כָּךְ (lesson 14).
Before a verb clause: אַחֲרֵי שֶׁ…
subtleties: אַחֲרֵי הַחַגִּים “after the holidays” is the Israeli way of postponing anything until the autumn holidays are over.

lexemes.note: “Until, till”; with מִ: from … to … (מִשְּׁמוֹנֶה עַד חָמֵשׁ). Before a clause עַד שֶׁ…

profile.feeling: Opening hours, deadlines, “see you tomorrow”.

senses.def: to, up to, as far as (a place, a number)

examples.tr: I am at work until five.
Until tomorrow! (see you tomorrow)

examples.text: הַדּוּחַ צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת מוּכָן עַד יוֹם שֵׁנִי.
examples.tr: The report has to be ready by Monday.

examples.text: מִתֵּל אָבִיב עַד חֵיפָה זֶה שָׁעָה.
examples.tr: From Tel Aviv to Haifa it’s an hour.

phrases.meaning: a wish for a long life (birthdays)

etymology.text: Biblical Hebrew; Wiktionary gives no etymology. The Aramaic word is the same: עַד.

funFacts: Unvowelled עד is also עֵד “witness” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: “From … to …” is מִ… עַד …: מִיּוֹם רִאשׁוֹן עַד יוֹם חֲמִישִׁי.
Before a verb clause use עַד שֶׁ…: עַד שֶׁהוּא בָּא.
subtleties: עַד can mean “until” or “by”: עַד מָחָר is “until tomorrow” or “by tomorrow” — the context decides (Wiktionary).

lexemes.note: “Since (a point in time)”, with the present for what is still going on: הוּא פֹּה מֵאָז יָנוּאָר. Alone it means “since then”. With a time word מִ alone also works: מֵהַבֹּקֶר “since the morning”.

profile.feeling: Since January, since then, ever since.

examples.tr: He has been here since January.
I have been waiting since the morning.
He hasn’t come back since then.

synonyms.nuance: “from, since” with a time word: מֵהַבֹּקֶר, מִיּוֹם רִאשׁוֹן
“from, since” in careful style: מִן הַבֹּקֶר

etymology.text: מִ “from” + אָז “then” (Wiktionary): “from then”.

funFacts: German seit + present (ich warte seit einer Stunde) works exactly like Hebrew מֵאָז + present.
pitfalls: A state that is still going on takes the present: הוּא פֹּה מֵאָז יָנוּאָר “he has been here since January” — like German Er ist seit Januar hier, not like English “has been”.
subtleties: Before a clause: מֵאָז שֶׁ… “ever since …” (Wiktionary).

lexemes.note: “During, for (a period)”: בְּמֶשֶׁךְ הַקַּיִץ “during the summer”, בְּמֶשֶׁךְ שָׁעָה “for an hour”. A length of time can also stand alone: מְחַכֶּה שָׁעָה.

profile.feeling: The whole stretch of a time.

examples.tr: During the summer the children are at Grandma’s.
During the week I (m.) work.
He waited for an hour.

synonyms.nuance: “during, at the time of” — a point inside the period: בִּזְמַן הָאֲרוּחָה

etymology.text: בְּ “in” + מֶשֶׁךְ “extent, duration” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: מֶשֶׁךְ comes from מָשַׁךְ “to pull, draw out” — a duration is time “drawn out”.
pitfalls: A length of time often needs no preposition at all: אֲנִי מְחַכֶּה שָׁעָה “I’ve been waiting an hour”.
It is one word: בְּמֶשֶׁךְ (be + meshekh), with a soft כ at the end.
subtleties: בְּמֶשֶׁךְ stresses the whole period; בִּזְמַן a moment inside it.
